messages.text: We manufacture laboratory freezers and buy a control board from two suppliers. One supplies about sixty percent and has offered an eighteen-month price reduction if we move nearly all volume to it. The savings would fund a badly needed reliability program. Its defect rate has been lower than the smaller supplier's, and it has never missed a shipment to us. Operations wants the simpler relationship. I am uneasy about concentrating a critical component, but paying more for worse current performance is not obviously prudent either.

It is worth stepping back to compare the entire operating system, rather than just pitting unit price against the abstract benefits of diversification. You should estimate the impact on quality, engineering support, working capital, and the effort required for qualification. Consider your recovery time after a potential disruption and how this shift in volume would change your bargaining position. It is also helpful to distinguish between an alternate supplier that is currently imperfect versus one that is fundamentally incapable of improving under a defined plan.

The smaller supplier caused two line stoppages last year, though both were resolved within a day. Maintaining its board requires separate firmware testing and an extra inspection step. My quality director says dual sourcing creates variation and consumes engineers who should be preventing freezer failures. Please do not assume two suppliers automatically means resilience; complexity has caused real defects for us.

That is a fair point; redundancy can sometimes introduce its own failure modes. The decision should really be about comparing tested recovery options—like inventory levels, commonality of design, access to tooling, and the time needed to bring a new supplier online—rather than just relying on the number of suppliers on your roster. You should measure the specific reliability program the savings would buy and determine if that investment mitigates larger product risks than the sourcing concentration itself creates.

The larger supplier will hold eight weeks of finished boards in a warehouse near our plant and give us quarterly access to its continuity plans. It assembles in two facilities, but both use the same semiconductor and both receive it through the same regional distributor. It says that component is standard and available from several manufacturers. Our engineers can keep the firmware interface documentation, but we do not own the board layout.

Having two assembly sites does not actually diversify you if they share the same upstream bottleneck, though the local inventory certainly buys you response time. You should verify the true substitutability of that semiconductor and clarify your rights during shortages. Also, confirm who owns the warehouse, who holds the insurance, and whether those stored boards will age or require firmware updates. While keeping the interface is good, the lack of layout ownership means even an emergency second source would require significant engineering and qualification work.

We asked the smaller supplier whether it would remain qualified at ten percent of volume. It says that level is uneconomic, but it would accept twenty-five percent if we commit for a year and jointly fix the inspection failures. That would cut the projected savings almost in half. Operations argues that a dormant backup is mostly theater anyway, and quality prefers either a meaningful improvement program or a clean exit.

They have a point; token volume often preserves a name without preserving actual capability. You should compare a seventy-five/twenty-five split against single sourcing combined with a funded requalification plan. If you go with the split, you must predefine target improvements for defects and delivery, with a clear exit strategy if they fail. For single sourcing, you need to establish exactly who can build what, using which files and tooling, and the precise elapsed time required—not just a vague assurance that another source exists.

Finance modeled both paths. The split still funds the most urgent reliability work, although not the full program. The larger supplier agreed that the local inventory belongs to us once produced and can be moved if the contract ends. The smaller supplier will let our engineer review its process monthly and credit the extra inspection cost until its defect rate reaches the agreed range. Neither contract requires exclusivity.

Those terms help convert abstract options into actual operating protections. The split keeps production knowledge alive while giving the smaller supplier a path to improve, and the owned inventory acts as a buffer against disruption. You should track the cost of engineering attention closely and set a hard decision date; otherwise, the improvement program could drag on indefinitely just because diversification feels like the right thing to do.

My concern now is that we are protecting against a dramatic disruption while accepting the ordinary defects we have already experienced. We propose two review points at six and twelve months. If the smaller supplier misses the quality or delivery thresholds at either review, new orders move to the primary supplier. If it passes, it keeps twenty-five percent. We would also complete a paper and practical recovery exercise using the interface files and stored boards.

That approach ensures the insurance is actually worth the cost. Be sure to define the sampling rules and thresholds before you start, and ensure a single outlier batch doesn't unfairly skew the results. The recovery exercise should test your decision authority, the logistics of moving the stock, and the time required to validate a replacement. The goal is to uncover any flawed assumptions now while you still have the luxury of time.

I will recommend the seventy-five/twenty-five split for one year, with the joint quality plan, owned buffer stock, two fixed supplier reviews, and the recovery exercise. The reliability program will start with its highest-risk items rather than waiting for every projected saving. If the secondary supplier fails the predefined thresholds, we will stop paying for a nominal backup. If it passes, we will have evidence that the extra complexity is controlled rather than simply hoping two sources are safer.

That recommendation treats diversification as a capability that must perform rather than a slogan, and it views concentration as a risk that can be managed rather than an automatic failure. You are keeping the ordinary quality costs, upstream dependencies, and recovery paths visible. Make sure to document the findings from the exercise so your next sourcing decision is based on actual performance data rather than the original theoretical arguments.

We performed the recovery exercise before signing. The stored boards could be moved, but a portion had older firmware and failed our current diagnostic on the first attempt. The problem was fixed in a day once engineering identified it. Operations called that a successful exercise; the quality director called it evidence that eight weeks of inventory is not eight weeks of usable protection. I think both readings are fair.

You should record both the initial failure and the resulting recovery time. The exercise succeeded as a learning experience, even if it failed as proof of immediate, plug-and-play usability. I recommend adding firmware status to your inventory controls, scheduling regular tests, and deciding how updates will be applied without depleting your buffer. This will make the stock more credible, but ensure you don't gloss over the initial failure when reporting on your overall readiness.

The primary supplier then asked for a rolling ninety-day forecast and first opportunity to quote any new board design. It says the lower price assumes planning visibility and engineering continuity. The clause is not exclusive, but our procurement manager thinks it could make the supplier the default before alternatives are considered. Finance says first opportunity costs nothing if we can reject the quote.

The risk here is procedural rather than formal. You should limit the response window, explicitly reserve the right to develop alternatives in parallel, and ensure no confidential competitor designs are leaked. Forecast visibility might improve supply, but you need to specify which changes are binding and whether the supplier can reduce allocation if forecasts are inaccurate. A default position can be efficient, but you must monitor it to prevent creeping path dependence.

At the six-month review, the smaller supplier met the defect threshold but required more of our engineer's time than expected. Its team says the attention is why quality improved; our engineer says several fixes are now stable and the next six months should be lighter. If we count all that time, the secondary source is more expensive than the contract comparison showed. If we treat the learning as a one-time investment, it may still be worthwhile.

It is important to separate recurring support costs from one-time capability-building efforts. Keep both in the ledger for now. You should test the claim that effort will decline at the twelve-month review instead of deciding today how to categorize the past. Furthermore, note whether the joint fixes actually improved your internal design or just the supplier's process; the option is more valuable if that knowledge transfers, but it is expensive if the performance is permanently subsidized by your engineering team.

We have now learned that the shared semiconductor package will be discontinued in eighteen months. Both board suppliers knew a change was likely, but neither had a firm date. The primary supplier proposes leading a common replacement design. The secondary wants to develop its own board, arguing that a shared design recreates the same upstream risk. I am frustrated that the event we were protecting against is not a supplier shutdown but a redesign both suppliers must navigate.

That definitely shifts the purpose of your split. You need to decide if resilience is best served by two independent redesign paths or by a single, well-governed design that both suppliers can manufacture. Two designs diversify your technical assumptions but double the validation and firmware work; one design minimizes variation but concentrates control. Whatever you choose, require milestone proof, clear ownership terms, and a fallback plan if things slip.

We will keep the seventy-five/twenty-five allocation through the twelve-month review, update and test the owned buffer, and count engineering support explicitly. For the replacement, we will fund a shared interface and validation specification while asking both suppliers to propose implementations; we will not give either an automatic design award. The first-opportunity clause will have a short deadline and no restriction on parallel work. At twelve months we will decide using quality, total support cost, redesign progress, and demonstrated recovery—not the original eighteen-percent headline.

The evolving evidence has shifted your goal from simply buying redundancy to maintaining adaptable production knowledge through a major component transition. This plan keeps competition alive without blindly assuming two implementations are safer, and it forces that hidden engineering work into the light. Make sure to archive the first recovery attempt, the forecast terms, the support ledger, and the redesign milestones. Those observations are far more informative now than either supplier's initial record or the abstract appeal of the original sourcing strategy.
